title: Distracted by Increase, Time, and the Crusher

paragraphs.text: This surah begins by describing a very common human weakness. Competing with one another for more and more worldly things keeps people busy and distracted, until they finally visit the graveyards. Then comes a firm warning, repeated twice for emphasis: no, you are going to know; then no, you are going to know. If only people knew with real certainty, they would live very differently. They will surely see the Hellfire. Then they will see it with the eye of certainty, so that no doubt remains. Finally, on that Day, they will be asked about every pleasure and blessing they enjoyed. The surah reminds the reader that the race for more possessions does not last, and that every comfort a person enjoys today will be the subject of a question tomorrow.

The next surah is very short, yet it carries a complete message. Allah swears by time. Indeed, all mankind is in a state of loss. There is only one exception: those who believe, do righteous deeds, advise one another to hold on to the truth, and advise one another to be patient. These four qualities together describe the people who are saved from loss. Two of them are about a person's own faith and actions, and two are about how believers help one another. Every passing moment of time is either a step toward loss or a step toward success, depending on how a person uses it.

The following surah begins with a strong warning: woe to every person who insults others and mocks them. Such a person gathers wealth and counts it again and again. He imagines that his money will make him live forever. But the answer is a firm "No!". He will surely be thrown into the Crusher. A question is then asked to show how terrible it is: what can make you know what the Crusher is? It is the fire of Allah, kept burning without end. The surah shows the connection between greed, arrogance toward others and a false sense of security. A person who trusts in his wealth and looks down on people forgets that his money cannot keep him alive, and that he will one day face the consequences of his behavior. These ayahs teach the reader to treat people with respect and not to treat wealth as a guarantee of safety.

hardWords.m: special force given to show importance
a firm promise that something will happen
